title: Fueling the Modern Endurance Athlete: The High-Carbohydrate Revolution, Exogenous Ketones, and an Evidence-Based Approach for the Sports Medicine Clinician.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Carbohydrate is the principal limiting fuel for prolonged, high-intensity endurance exercise, and consensus guidelines have long capped recommended intake during exercise at approximately 90 g/h. Two developments have challenged and extended contemporary fueling practice: a shift toward carbohydrate intakes of 100 to 150 g/h in elite endurance sport, and widespread commercial availability of exogenous ketone supplements marketed as ergogenic aids. Both have outpaced the clinical evidence and have reached the competitive and recreational athletes who present to sports medicine clinicians.
EVIDENCE ACQUISITION: Narrative review of primary metabolic and performance studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and consensus statements published through mid-2026, identified through PubMed and reference tracing.
STUDY DESIGN: Narrative review.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 5.
RESULTS: Multiple-transportable-carbohydrate formulations (glucose plus fructose) raise exogenous carbohydrate oxidation above the roughly 1 g/minute ceiling imposed by intestinal glucose transport, providing the mechanistic basis for fueling rates of ≥90 g/h. Ingesting 120 g/h increases exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, but the best-controlled studies have not demonstrated additional endogenous (liver and muscle) glycogen sparing or a consistent performance advantage, and gastrointestinal tolerability requires deliberate gut training. For exogenous ketones, an influential 2016 study reported altered substrate use and improved time-trial performance. Subsequent trials and multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses have not confirmed an acute ergogenic effect, and several have documented gastrointestinal distress or impaired performance. The more promising and reproducible signal for ketones lies in postexercise recovery and attenuation of overreaching. Finally, athletes who restrict in-competition and training carbohydrate to pursue leanness risk low energy and carbohydrate availability, the substrate of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs).
CONCLUSION: Carbohydrate intake of ≤90 g/h, built through progressive gut training, is supported by consensus guidelines and mechanistic evidence for prolonged, high-intensity endurance events; progression toward 120 g/h is reasonable in selected, well-adapted athletes competing in the longest events, with the understanding that a performance benefit >90 g/h remains unproven. Routine exogenous ketone supplementation for acute performance is not supported by current evidence; a recovery-focused application is plausible and increasingly supported but requires further study. Clinicians should frame both strategies within adequate energy availability to protect long-term athlete health.Strength-of-Recommendation Taxonomy (SORT):B.

title: Paraspinal Muscle Quality and Functional Outcomes Following Lumbar Fusion: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) procedures are associated with postoperative paraspinal muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration (FI), which may influence long-term pain and functional recovery. However, the relationship between muscle quality, both pre- and postoperatively, and patient-reported outcomes remains unclear for patients undergoing lumbar fusion. This correlation was compared between minimally invasive surgery (MIS) and conventional open surgery (COS) approaches to assess differences in postoperative muscle preservation and functional outcomes.
METHODS: A systematic review, conducted following PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250650064), examined studies found in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through February 2025. Studies were included if they assessed adult patients undergoing LIF with preoperative CT or MRI evaluation of the multifidus (MF) or erector spinae (ES) and reported postoperative cross-sectional area (CSA), FI, or patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).
RESULTS: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria; risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for 19 non-randomized studies and RoB 2 for one randomized trial. Seven of nine COS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, including all three COS-only studies, measured by CSA and FI. Two of twelve MIS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, with four of six direct comparisons found smaller declines in CSA, increases in FI, or both after MIS compared to COS in at least one muscle or setting. Higher preoperative muscle quality, particularly lower FI, and smaller pre- to postoperative muscle changes were associated with greater PROM improvements. Across the PROM-focused studies, four of the five reported that higher preoperative CSA or lower FI predicted better postoperative improvements in functional outcomes, with one identifying that MF FI of 61% or greater as a threshold for failing to achieve clinically meaningful ODI improvements.
CONCLUSION: MIS techniques were associated with a decrease in pre- to postoperative FI compared with COS, although PROM improvement occurred across both approaches. While preoperative paraspinal muscle quality and size decreases are generally smaller with better functional outcomes following postoperative LIF, this relationship is not consistently observed across all studies or surgical techniques. These findings suggest that the current imaging-based biomarkers may not fully capture the multifactorial nature of functional recovery and underscore the need for further research into additional predictors of muscle recovery.

title: Diagnosis, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport after Athletic Hamstring Injury: An ICCUS Society Consensus Statement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athletic hamstring injuries (AHSI) remain a persistent challenge because recurrence is common and clinical decisions often depend on incomplete evidence. This consensus statement is intended to give clinicians a practical, unified framework for classification, rehabilitation, and return to sport after athletic hamstring injury. The purpose of this study was to achieve expert consensus on the management of athletic hamstring injuries through a structured, scientific survey approach.
STUDY DESIGN: Delphi Survey.
METHODS: A modified Delphi process, aligned with CREDES guidelines, was conducted with an expert panel of sports physical therapists identified as having specific expertise in AHSI from the ICCUS Society. Consensus was defined a priori as at least 80% agreement or disagreement on a 5-point Likert scale. Statements addressed three areas: AHSI examination and classification, rehabilitation and management, and return to sport (RTS) testing.
RESULTS: Sixty statements were developed across three domains. Seventeen experienced clinicians completed the final round. Overall, 54 statements reached consensus, with a mean Likert score of 4.56 ± 0.37 out of 5 (strongly agree), and mean agreement of 89.88% ± 12.1%. Experts supported standardized terminology, MRI and the use of diagnostic ultrasound for diagnosis when appropriate, individualized and criterion-based rehabilitation, progressive tissue loading and length restoration, early neuromuscular control, gradual running and agility progression, progression to pain-free sprinting, objective strength assessment, sport-specific workloads, and athlete readiness as key RTS criteria.
DISCUSSION: The findings emphasize active rehabilitation guided by measurable progress rather than reliance on fixed thresholds. Clinicians should combine injury classification, functional presentation, symptom response, objective testing, sport demands, and athlete confidence when advancing rehabilitation and making RTS decisions.
CONCLUSION: This ICCUS Society consensus statement offers a practical roadmap for managing AHSI: classify clearly, load progressively, monitor symptoms, test objectively, and return athletes only when sport-specific running, sprinting, strength, training tolerance, and readiness align.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Post-Treatment Follow-up, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport: Proceedings of the International Consensus Meetings on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle.
abstract: BackgroundPostoperative follow-up, rehabilitation, and return to sport (RTS) are key components of recovery following surgical management of osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLT). However, substantial variability exists in postoperative protocols, with limited high-quality evidence guiding clinical practicesMethodsInternational experts convened during the International Congress on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle (ICCRA) in Pittsburgh, USA (2017), with subsequent ratification of recommendations in New York, USA (2025). The original consensus statements were developed using a modified Delphi process involving electronic surveys, structured questionnaires, and expert discussion. Consensus strength was defined as consensus (51%-74%), strong consensus (75%-99%), or unanimous (100%). The recommendations addressed postoperative follow-up, rehabilitation, and RTS following OLT management.ResultsA total of 16 consensus statements were developed and subsequently ratified, comprising 7 statements addressing post-treatment follow-up and 9 addressing rehabilitation and RTS. All statements achieved strong consensus, with agreement ranging from 75% to 98%. Follow-up recommendations emphasized standardized clinical assessment and patient-reported outcomes, with extended monitoring in select patients. Rehabilitation recommendations supported early controlled motion and progressive weightbearing, with individualized progression according to procedure and clinical performance. Return to sport recommendations emphasized functional recovery and individualized decision-making. Ten statements (63%) were classified exclusively as Grade E, highlighting the limited evidence supporting several recommendations.ConclusionThe ICCRA consensus statements establish a structured framework for postoperative follow-up, rehabilitation, and RTS following surgical management of OLT. Despite strong expert agreement, several recommendations remain supported by limited evidence, underlining the need for prospective studies to establish validated, procedure-specific rehabilitation protocols and objective RTS criteria.Level of Evidence:V, expert consensus.

title: Hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement in American football athletes: examining factors associated with outcomes at a mean follow-up time of 6.3 years.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Femoroacetabular impingement (FAIS) is a common cause of hip pain and performance limitation in athletes. Hip arthroscopy is the gold standard of treatment in professional American football athletes, with numerous studies demonstrating favorable outcomes and high return-to-sport (RTS) rates. However, limited outcomes data exists in collegiate athletes and fewer still in high school athletes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate long-term patient-reported outcomes (PROs), RTS rates, and predictors of outcomes following hip arthroscopy for symptomatic FAIS in high school and collegiate football athletes.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed which included high-school and collegiate football athletes who underwent hip arthroscopy for symptomatic FAIS. Outcomes were assessed using the modified Harris Hip Score (mHHS), International Hip Outcome Tool-12 (IHOT-12), and Hip Outcomes Score-Sport Specific Subscale (HOS-Sport). Data regarding return to preinjury sport were also collected. Pre-operative radiographic data, including alpha angle, lateral center edge angle, and Tönnis grade, were collected.
RESULTS: This cohort had a mean post-operative follow up of 6.3 years, with mean PRO scores of 82.2 on the mHHS, 84.6 on the iHOT-12, and 88.3 on the HOS-Sport. PASS thresholds were achieved by 69%, 77% and 80% of athletes for the same outcomes, respectively. 60% of the cohort attempted to return to sport, and 91% of the athletes who attempted to return to preinjury level of sport were successful. Increased age at time of surgery and larger pre-operative alpha angles were associated with worse PRO scores at follow-up.
CONCLUSIONS: Hip arthroscopy for FAIS in high school and collegiate football players yielded favorable long-term outcomes and RTS rates. This is similar to current outcomes data in professional athletes. Increased alpha angle and age at surgery were associated with worse outcomes, emphasizing the importance of early recognition and appropriate surgical treatment. Comparisons of outcomes between blocking and nonblocking positions may warrant further investigation in larger cohorts.

title: Optimizing Post-operative Analgesia for Early Rehabilitation after Orthopedic Knee Surgery: A Randomized Comparison of Adductor Canal, Infiltration between the Popliteal Artery and Capsule of the Posterior Knee and Genicular Nerve Blocks.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Orthopedic knee surgery, including anterior cruciate ligament tear repair, patellar fracture fixation, and surgery for knee osteoarthritis, is often followed by moderate to severe pain that delays early mobilization, quadriceps activation, and physiotherapy. Motor-sparing, opioid-sparing analgesia is therefore preferred. Ultrasound-guided adductor canal block (ACB), infiltration between the popliteal artery and capsule of the posterior knee (IPACK) block, and genicular nerve block (GNB) are three such options, but direct comparisons in orthopedic knee surgery are limited.
AIMS: To compare the post-operative analgesic efficacy of ultrasound-guided ACB, IPACK block, and GNB in patients undergoing knee surgeries under subarachnoid block.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective, randomized, single-blind comparative study was conducted in the Department of Anaesthesiology, N.S.C.B. Medical College and Hospital, Jabalpur, over 18 months after institutional ethics committee approval (IEC/2023/7335-1). Ninety-nine ASA physical status I-II patients aged 18-60 years scheduled for elective knee surgery were randomized equally into three groups (n = 33 each). Group A received ultrasound-guided ACB, Group I received ultrasound-guided IPACK block, and Group G received ultrasound-guided GNB. Each block was performed with 20 mL of 0.375% ropivacaine, followed by standardized spinal anesthesia. Post-operative pain was assessed using a Visual Analog Scale (VAS) over 24 h. Time to rescue intravenous paracetamol, tramadol requirement, and block-related complications were recorded.
RESULTS: Baseline demographic characteristics were comparable among groups. Group G had lower mean VAS scores at most post-operative time points, including 16, 20 and 24 h. The time to first rescue paracetamol was longest in Group G (5.87 ± 0.43 h), followed by Group A (5.62 ± 0.48 h) and Group I (5.42 ± 0.49 h). The second paracetamol dose was also delayed the longest in Group G (11.79 ± 0.83 h). Tramadol was required in 6.06% of patients in Group G, compared with 21.21% in Group A and 30.30% in Group I.
CONCLUSION: In patients undergoing orthopedic knee surgery, all three ultrasound-guided motor-sparing blocks provided clinically useful post-operative analgesia. GNB was associated with lower pain scores at most intervals, delayed rescue analgesic requirement, and reduced tramadol use compared with ACB and IPACK block, making it a promising option to support early rehabilitation. Larger adequately powered trials with procedure-specific subgroup analysis and functional outcomes, such as quadriceps strength and range of motion, are warranted.

title: Upper-Extremity Tendinopathy and Enthesopathy in the Athlete: Best Evidence in Diagnostic and Therapeutic Advances.
abstract: Tendinopathy and enthesopathy represent common overuse conditions in athletic populations and frequently affect the upper extremity, particularly the rotator cuff, elbow extensor origin, and wrist extensors. These conditions arise predominantly from mechanical overload and are characterized clinically by load-dependent pain and impaired function. Following clinical evaluation, diagnostic evaluation frequently requires multimodality to exclude alternative pathology or inflammatory disease. Exercise-based rehabilitation remains the foundation of management, with contemporary evidence supporting progressive, individualized loading programs, including eccentric, concentric, isometric, and heavy slow resistance protocols, are tailored to symptom severity and sport-specific demands. Adjunctive modalities such as extracorporeal shock wave therapy demonstrate benefit in select chronic cases, particularly lateral epicondylitis and calcific shoulder tendinopathy. Although nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs and corticosteroid injections may provide short-term symptom relief, corticosteroids are associated with inferior long-term outcomes and potential deleterious effects on tendon structure. Biologic therapies, including platelet-rich plasma and topical glyceryl trinitrate, demonstrate heterogeneous results, and high-volume image-guided injections remain selectively used in refractory cases. Surgical intervention is reserved for patients with persistent symptoms following 6 to 12 months of comprehensive nonoperative care because most individuals achieve symptom resolution without operative management. Open, arthroscopic, and percutaneous techniques demonstrate comparable outcomes. Emerging technologies, including in-office nanoarthroscopy and bioinductive collagen scaffolds, show early promise but require further high-quality investigation.

title: Platelet-related extracellular vesicles: Therapeutic roles in musculoskeletal disorders.
abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders are a major cause of pain, disability, and loss of function. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated for musculoskeletal repair, and interest has increasingly extended to extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations obtained from platelet-related starting materials. These include EV-enriched preparations collected from isolated platelets or defined platelet concentrates (P-EVs), from PRP (PRP-EVs), and from platelet lysate (PL-EVs). They do not represent the same biological product. Their cellular contributors, co-isolated soluble components, and molecular composition can differ substantially, and the name of the starting material does not prove the origin of every vesicle in the preparation. Preclinical studies nevertheless suggest that these EV preparations can influence inflammatory responses, cartilage metabolism, tendon-cell behavior, and the local repair environment. The strength of this evidence varies with the source material, separation and characterization methods, experimental model, and delivery strategy. This review examines the therapeutic evidence for platelet-related EV preparations in musculoskeletal disorders, while keeping P-EVs, PRP-EVs, PL-EVs, and plasma-derived EVs distinct and considering the methodological limitations that currently restrict comparison and clinical translation.

title: Infrared thermography reveals differences in thigh skin-temperature trajectories during early recovery after four cycling protocols.
abstract: Exercise intensity or mode alters metabolic heat production, blood-flow distribution, and heat dissipation, but the evolution of these thermal responses during early recovery remains unclear. In this randomized crossover study, 19 adults (10 men, 9 women) completed low-intensity continuous cycling (E1), moderate-intensity continuous cycling (E2), high-intensity intervals (E3), and all-out sprint intervals (E4). Infrared thermography measured average skin temperature (aTsk) in a standardized thigh region through 15 min of recovery. At 15 min, changes from each session's baseline were -0.12, +0.13, -1.19, and -1.86 °C after E1-E4, respectively. The condition-by-stage interaction was significant (F(5.45, 92.68) = 17.38, P < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.506). Absolute aTsk was lower after E3 and E4 than after E1 by 1.04 °C (95% confidence interval 0.68-1.39) and 1.36 °C (0.98-1.74), respectively (both Bonferroni-adjusted P < 0.001). None of the condition-adjusted Pearson correlations passed FDR correction, consistent with substantial between-condition contributions. Thermograms from one participant also illustrated local surface thermal contrast. Early-recovery thermography is a candidate measure of responses to these complete cycling protocols, pending prospective within-person validation. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ChiCTR2400089036, retrospectively registered.

title: Traumatic brain injury, symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction in former elite rugby players.
abstract: While self-reported repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure in former athletes has been associated with symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction, it is uncertain whether these symptoms are mediated by changes in brain structure. We used cross-sectional data from 57 middle-aged, cognitively healthy, former elite rugby players and 114 propensity-matched controls. Questionnaires were used to collect self-reported traumatic brain injury (srTBI: blows to the head; episodes of feeling dazed and confused; episodes of loss of consciousness), RHI exposure (career length, play at the highest level and playing position), medical history, symptoms of depression (Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression scale) and sleep dysfunction (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). Grey matter volumes and diffusion tensor imaging measures were obtained using FreeSurfer (v7.1.0, v7.4.2) and FSL (v6.0.5). We assessed how srTBI, RHI exposure, symptoms of depression, sleep dysfunction and the imaging markers were related using Spearman correlations, multivariate regression models and partial least squares structural equation modelling. Although former rugby players reported a higher number of blows to the head (9.8 versus 5.4, P < 0.001), number of episodes of feeling dazed and confused (4.5 versus 1.7, P < 0.001) and number of episodes of loss of consciousness (1.9 versus 0.7, P < 0.001), they were less likely to report a past diagnosis of anxiety (7% versus 22%, P = 0.03) or sleep disorders (2% versus 15%, P = 0.02) than controls. In rugby players, srTBI correlated poorly with RHI exposure. Furthermore, srTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with previous depression, anxiety and sleep disorders. Higher srTBI was directly associated with more symptoms of depression [B: 0.52 (95%CI: 0.21-0.74)], and indirectly associated with more sleep dysfunction [B: 0.18 (95%CI: 0.03-0.39)], fully mediated through symptoms of depression. Higher srTBI was also associated with a larger putamen (r = 0.28, P = 0.03) and inferior-tubular hypothalamus (r = 0.35, P = 0.007), thicker medial orbitofrontal (r = 0.32, P = 0.02) and insular cortices (r = 0.40, P = 0.002), lower axial diffusivity of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (r = -0.28, P = 0.03) and uncinate fasciculus (r = -0.26, P = 0.048), lower fractional anisotropy (r = -0.44, P < 0.001) and higher radial diffusivity (r = 0.29, P = 0.03) of the tapetum. Symptoms of depression were associated with thicker superior (r = 0.30, P = 0.02) and inferior (r = 0.33, P = 0.01) parietal cortices, higher fractional anisotropy of the hippocampal cingulum (r = 0.27, P = 0.04) and lower mean diffusivity of the fornix (r = -0.28, P = 0.03). None of these imaging markers mediated the association between srTBI and symptoms of depression. SrTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with symptoms of depression in former rugby players. However, this relationship was not mediated through differences in brain structure, suggesting that psychosocial or methodological factors such as recall bias and common method bias may be more important.

title: Developmental Differences in Muscle, Tendon, and Cartilage Injuries in Elite Badminton.
abstract: This study investigated severe muscle, tendon, and cartilage injury characteristics by injury timing and post-injury management among elite badminton players. A retrospective interview study was conducted with 126 badminton players aged 19-24 years. A total of 87 severe injury cases reported by 73 athletes were analyzed, with some athletes contributing more than one case. Injuries were classified by timing into the secondary school group (SSG, n = 33) and the post-secondary group (PSG, n = 54). Injury characteristics and post-injury management were compared using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests, with effect sizes. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) examined associations with injury timing. Compared with the SSG, the PSG had higher odds of lower limb muscle injuries (OR = 6.00, 95% CI = 1.85-19.47, p = .003) and smash/stroke-related injuries (OR = 5.43, 95% CI = 1.15-25.66, p = .033), whereas the PSG had lower odds of lower limb tendinopathies (OR = 0.21, 95% CI = 0.08-0.55, p = .001). These findings suggest that severe injury characteristics may differ according to the timing of injury occurrence, despite no significant between-group differences in post-injury management, and may help inform potential injury prevention priorities based on the observed injury patterns.

title: Prevalence and predictors of in-class dozing among collegiate athletes and non-athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adequate sleep is critical for recovery and performance, yet athletes often experience less sleep than non-athletes, potentially impacting their academic performance. This study investigates the prevalence and factors in-class dozing among collegiate athletes compared to non-athletes.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study surveyed 165 athletes and 92 non-athletes using an anonymous online questionnaire, focusing on sleep duration, commute times, part-time employment, and attitudes towards sleeping in class.
RESULTS: Athletes reported a higher frequency of in-class dozing (70.4%) compared to non-athletes (55.5%, P=0.009). The primary reason for in-class dozing among athletes was fatigue from sports practice, whereas non-athletes attributed it to part-time work. Logistic regression analysis revealed that athletes had a higher risk of in-class dozing (OR=2.71, 95% CI 1.42-5.16, P=0.002), and both younger age (OR=0.46, 95% CI 0.24-0.87, P=0.016) and insufficient sleep at night (OR=0.71, 95% CI 0.55-0.92, P=0.010) were associated with increased risk.
CONCLUSIONS: Both athletes and non-athletes are not obtaining adequate sleep, with athletes particularly affected by training-related fatigue possibly causing in-class dozing. Factors contributing to the likelihood of in-class dozing included younger age, inadequate nightly sleep, being an athlete, and engagement in part-time employment.

title: Autologous Osteochondral Transplantation Remains a Reliable Option for Talar Osteochondral Lesions, With Low Knee Donor-Site Morbidity.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Autologous osteochondral transplantation (AOT) is a surgical option for talar osteochondral lesions (OCL), with favorable outcomes and high return-to-sport rates; however, knee donor-site morbidity remains a concern.
PURPOSE: To evaluate clinical and functional outcomes, complications, return to work and sport, and satisfaction after AOT for talar OCL.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective case series.
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients ≥18 years with talar OCL treated with AOT (2011-2022; minimum 2-year follow-up); patients with prior knee pain or surgery, infection, advanced osteoarthritis, or rheumatologic disease were excluded. Outcomes included the AOFAS hindfoot, Lysholm, and Tegner scores, ankle and knee visual analog scale (VAS) pain, satisfaction, return to work and sport, and complications.
RESULTS: Thirty-seven patients (78% male; median age, 36 years; median follow-up, 24 months) were included. Median lesion size was 150 mm², all medial; 14 (38%) had concomitant procedures. The AOFAS score improved from 54.5 to 95.8 (mean difference, 41.3; 95% CI, 38.4-44.3) and ankle VAS from 7.0 to 1.6 (-5.4; 95% CI, -5.9 to -4.9) (both p < 0.001). Postoperative Lysholm score was 98.8 ± 4.0 and knee VAS 1.2 ± 0.8 (no preoperative knee scores). Return to work took 2.3 ± 1.2 months; all 32 athletes resumed sport at 6.5 ± 2.1 months, 20 (63%) in their pre-injury sport. Tegner scores were unchanged (5.4 vs 5.5; p = 0.624). One knee hemarthrosis and one repeat ankle arthroscopy occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: AOT for talar OCL yielded favorable short-term outcomes, high return-to-work and return-to-sport rates, and low reported knee donor-site morbidity; baseline knee scores were unavailable.
LEVEL OF CLINICAL EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Unpacking the Success: An Ecological Systems Perspective on Distance Running Performance in Ethiopia.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study employed a mixed-methods approach grounded in Ecological Systems Theory to investigate factors contributing to Ethiopia's dominance in distance running.
METHODS: Data were collected from 145 Ethiopian distance runners (87 male, 58 female; mean age = 22.4 ± 3.1 years) using questionnaires, semi-structured interviews (n = 24), AQ1 and focus groups (n = 8).
RESULTS: Quantitative analysis revealed that, in multivariable logistic regression, primary education level (odds ratio [OR] = 5.80, q < 0.005, where q is the false discovery rate [FDR]-adjusted P-value), 10th/12th certificate (OR = 0.20, q = 0.016), normal body mass index (OR = 2.85, q = 0.021), and academy training (OR = 2.40, q = 0.044) maintained statistical significance at q < 0.05, while recovery practices (OR = 2.38, q = 0.051) and centre-based training (OR = 2.23, q = 0.060) remained significant at q < 0.10. Qualitative analysis yielded three core themes: (1) The Forged Resilience: Hardship as an Unseen Training Ground; (2) The Weight of a Nation: Community as Support and Pressure; and (3) The Crossroads: Tradition Versus Modernization in Training. Integration showed that quantitative predictors were profoundly shaped by socioeconomic realities, with the "primary education" finding explained by athletes' physically demanding rural lifestyles.
CONCLUSIONS: Ethiopian distance running success is a multifaceted phenomenon embedded within a complex system of community support, organizational culture, and socioeconomic background. Sustaining success requires systemic interventions extending well beyond individual athletes to strengthen the entire ecosystem in which Ethiopian champions are made.

title: The Impact of Tourniquet Duration on Postoperative Opioid Use and Recovery After Total Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tourniquet use during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains common, but its effects on postoperative pain, opioid use, and stiffness are unclear. We evaluated whether tourniquet duration was associated with pain- and stiffness-related outcomes after primary TKA.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective study of 17,850 adults undergoing primary unilateral TKA at a single center from March 2016 to June 2023. Tourniquet use was categorized by inflation time relative to operative time as no tourniquet (n = 1,243), partial tourniquet (less than 0.6; n = 2,914), tourniquet-until-arthrotomy-closure (≥ 0.6 to less than 1; n = 10,003), or full-duration tourniquet (≥ 1; n = 3,690). The primary outcome was postoperative pain assessed by postoperative inpatient and cumulative 90-day morphine milligram equivalents (MME). The secondary outcomes were hours to clear physical therapy (PT), manipulation under anesthesia (MUA) within 120 days, and patient-reported Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS JR) at six weeks. Multivariable regressions adjusted for covariates. The no-tourniquet group served as the reference.
RESULTS: Partial-tourniquet use was associated with lower 90-day opioid consumption (-90 MME; 95% confidence interval (CI) -150 to -30; P = 0.003). Tourniquet-until-closure and full-duration tourniquet were associated with higher inpatient opioid consumption (+10 MMEs; 95% CI, 2 to 17; P = 0.015; and +14 MMEs; 95% CI, 6 to 22; P = 0.001), longer time to PT clearance (+2.7 hours, 95% CI, 1.0 to 4.5; P = 0.002; and +4.1 hours, 95% CI, 2.2 to 5.9; P < 0.001), and higher adjusted odds (OR) of MUA (OR 1.78, 95% CI, 1.14 to 2.79; P = 0.012; and OR 1.64, 95% CI, 1.02 to 2.64; P = 0.040). Partial-tourniquet use was not associated with increased time to clear PT or increased odds of MUA. The KOOS JR scores did not differ significantly across strategies.
CONCLUSIONS: Tourniquet use during TKA showed duration-dependent associations with postoperative outcomes. Partial-tourniquet use may represent a balanced strategy, associated with lower cumulative 90-day opioid consumption without the delayed PT clearance or increased MUA risk observed with longer-duration tourniquet strategies.

title: Orthopedic Surgeon and Primary Care Orthopedic Physician Preferences for Sports Participation for Cast-Immobilized Healing Fractures: A Survey.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: No published clinical practice guidelines outlining recommended activity restrictions were found for patients with cast-immobilized healing fractures; wide variations in practice exist. This survey aimed to elucidate physician/surgeon preferences for sports participation for patients with short arm cast-immobilized distal radial metaphyseal fractures.
METHODS: Attending orthopedic surgeons, physiatrists, and primary care sports medicine physicians at a single urban tertiary-care orthopedic hospital were invited to complete an anonymous survey with up to 26 questions from 5/2023-7/2023. Descriptive statistics were done. Pearson Chi-Square tests compared pediatric surgeons to all other providers.
RESULTS: One hundred twenty physicians and surgeons were invited to participate. Response rate was 43% (51/120); 59% (30/51) reported treating distal radial fractures with casting and were invited to complete the remaining survey; 70% (21/30) allow return to sports while casted. For respondents permitting sports/activity participation, factors impacting this decision included longer healing time from injury, minimal displacement, greater radiographic healing, and older age at the time of injury. Type of activity, effect on quality of life, level of competition, effect on college/team recruitment, and patient and parental pressure were noted factors impacting activity recommendations. Comparing pediatric orthopedic surgeons with all other providers, there was no notable difference in proportion permitting return to sport/activity in cast (63% vs. 73%, P = 0.67).
CONCLUSION: For cast-immobilized healing fractures of the distal radius, many physicians/surgeons permit sport/activity participation in some capacity, with multiple variables impacting providers preference for activity restrictions. Clinical practice guidelines delineating activity restrictions for cast-immobilized fractures should be developed.

title: Efficacy of Apparent Diffusion Coefficient Sampling in Muscle Tears and Intersex Differences in Professional Football Players: A Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the gold standard for monitoring the evolution of muscle injuries in athletes, although no established quantitative measure of recovery currently exists.
HYPOTHESIS: Apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values may provide a quantitative measure of muscle healing, and sex-related differences may exist in the evolution of muscle injuries.
STUDY DESIGN: Single-center retrospective observational cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2a.
METHODS: Twenty-six professional football (soccer) players (13 male ,13 female) undergoing MRI for muscle injury were retrospectively selected between October 2020 and June 2024. All athletes underwent MRI at baseline (T0) and at 2-week follow-up, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) acquisitions with b values of 0-100-800 s/mm². Two musculoskeletal radiologists measured ADC values within the index lesions at each examination. Changes in ADC between the two time points (ΔADC) were assessed using a paired-samples t test, while sex-related differences were evaluated using the Mann-Whitney U test.
RESULTS: The overall mean ADC value at the lesion site decreased from 2.06 ± 0.35 mm2/s at T0 to 1.61 ± 0.30 mm2/s at follow-up corresponding to a mean ΔADC of 0.44 ± 0.20 and a 21.84% reduction. The difference between T0 and follow-up was statistically significant (t = 8.12; P < 0.001). Mean ΔADC values were 0.32 ± 0.20 mm²/s in male players and 0.56 ± 0.25 mm²/s in female players, respectively, with a statistically significant difference between sexes (z = -2.95; P = 0.003). When only hamstring injuries were considered, female players showed a significantly greater decrease in ADC over time than male players (Mann-Whitney U test; exact P = 0.02), with mean ΔADC values of 0.56 ± 0.30 and 0.26 ± 0.08 mm²/s, respectively.
CONCLUSION: Muscle injury is associated with an acute increase in ADC values followed by a progressive decrease during healing. ADC may therefore represent a quantitative imaging biomarker for monitoring muscle recovery.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: ADC measurement within muscle tears may provide a quantitative assessment of healing status and support individualized rehabilitation strategies in athletes. Sex-related differences may exist in injury pathophysiology and recovery patterns relevant to safe return to play.

title: Discriminant and Prognostic Validity of the Multimodal Exertional Test (MET) for Athletes with Concussion.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exertional tests have become an informative tool to assist with clinical concussion management and return-to-sport medical decisions. However, current tests are resource intensive and thus, we developed a widely accessible, multimodal exertional test (MET). The objectives of this study were: (1) To evaluate the discriminant validity of the MET by examining sex-stratified differences in symptoms, heart rate (HR), and performance metrics between concussed and healthy athletes; and (2) To assess the predictive (prognostic) validity of the MET by determining whether week 1 MET performance predicts time to medical clearance.
METHODS: This study was conducted at a single academic institution and affiliated sport medicine clinic in Toronto, Canada, with participants recruited between August 2022 and November 2024. 115 interuniversity athletes (female n=49, male n=66) completed the MET at off-season and 55 interuniversity athletes with concussion (female n=37, male n=18) completed the MET up to six times at 1-, 2-, 3-, 4-, 6-, and 8-weeks post-injury. Average and maximum HR, symptoms, performance metrics, and MET pass/fail status were measured prior to and during the protocol. Probabilistic hierarchical models were implemented to estimate differences between concussion and healthy athletes (discriminant validity) and negative binomial analyses were used to examine whether MET performance predicted time to medical clearance (predictive validity).
RESULTS: At 1-week post injury, concussed athletes exhibited greater symptom provocation during the MET compared to healthy athletes, with differences after each task. MET failure rates were highest during weeks 1 (63%) and 2 (49%) and declined through week 8. Athletes who passed the MET at week 1 recovered 20.6 days faster (90% Credible Interval [CrI] = 4.9-36.8 days, posterior probability [pprob] > 0 = 97.7%) than those who failed.
CONCLUSION: The MET demonstrates discriminant validity by eliciting greater symptom provocation in athletes with concussion compared to healthy athletes. Improvements in symptoms and completion rates over 8 weeks indicate recovery-related gains in exertional tolerance. The MET also demonstrates predictive validity, as passing the test at week 1 was associated with faster time to medical clearance, supporting its potential utility as an early prognostic tool in concussion management.

title: Athletes and Medical Staff in Elite Contact Sports: a Quantitative Analysis of Use, Knowledge, and Attitudes Regarding Cannabinoids.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cannabis use among elite contact sport athletes increases with legal reform and commercial availability. Limited education in cannabinoid pharmacology, use, and risk persists among athletes and medical staff, fostering stigma and reducing evidence-based guidance and communication.
HYPOTHESIS: Athletes use cannabis but perceive stigma and discomfort discussing cannabis with medical staff.
STUDY DESIGN: Quantitative, descriptive cross-sectional surveys.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4.
METHODS: Two anonymous online surveys were administered to elite and professional contact sport athletes (Canada, United States, Australia) and medical and training staff (February 2023 to July 2024). Descriptive statistics assessed demographics, use patterns, knowledge, education needs, attitudes, stigma, communication, and league policies.
RESULTS: A total of 166 athletes (89.7% male, 35.2% aged 18-23 years) and 64 medical staff (physicians, athletic therapists, strength and conditioning coaches, etc) responded. Knowledge (pharmacology, interactions, dosing) was low. Overall, 56% of athletes currently used cannabinoids (81% having ever used), but only 21.7% knew the endocannabinoid system and 67.4% were unfamiliar with therapeutic dosing. Among medical staff, 59.5% were unfamiliar with mechanisms, only 14% were familiar with dosing protocols, and 71.4% lacked confidence in making treatment plans. Of the athletes, 86.5% believed cannabis had therapeutic value, 72.3% wanted education, and 74.1% favored qualified scientists as instructors. Of the medical staff, 79.5% reported strong educational need, with 100% of staff desiring athlete-specific cannabinoid education. Stigma and communication barriers were substantial: 81.3% of athletes perceived public stigma, 66.1% perceived staff stigma, and only 21.4% felt comfortable discussing cannabis with medical staff. Staff believed athletes would be honest if approached; however, <50% believed athletes trusted them enough to start the conversation. Both athletes and medical staff categorized cannabinoids as supplements or medications (unlike street drugs) and both supported legalization and a revision and update on league cannabis policies.
CONCLUSION: Athletes and medical staff exhibit parallel knowledge gaps and strong educational needs amid high interest, use, and significant communication barriers. Evidence-informed education and stigma-reducing strategies are urgently needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Athletes increasingly use cannabinoids for pain, sleep, and recovery, while medical staff report insufficient training and low confidence. System-level education, communication, and policy updates may improve safety, decision-making, and trust.

title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks.
DESIGN: Prospective study.
SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported.
PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes.
RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042).
CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

title: Comparison of immediate post-operative pain and functional outcomes of surgeon-administered adductor canal block through subvastus versus medial parapatellar approach in total knee arthroplasty: A retrospective comparative study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Post-operative pain significantly impedes early rehabilitation after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). The adductor canal block (ACB) provides effective analgesia with minimal quadriceps impairment. This study compares immediate post-operative pain and functional outcomes of surgeon-administered ACB through subvastus (SV) versus medial parapatellar (MP) approaches.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective comparative study conducted between January 2024 and March 2025, medical records of 60 patients who underwent unilateral primary TKA were reviewed. Patients were grouped based on the surgical approach used for intraoperative surgeon-administered ACB (30 SV, 30 MP). A modified anatomical technique was used in all cases. A standardized multimodal non-opioid post-operative analgesic protocol was used in both groups. Outcomes assessed at 12 h post-operatively included Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), timed up and go (TUG) test, and range of motion (ROM). Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 8.4.2.
RESULT: Both groups demonstrated significant post-operative improvement in pain and function. The SV group achieved superior pain control (post-operative VAS 3.52 ± 0.69 vs. 4.38 ± 0.82; P = 0.0001), better functional outcomes (WOMAC 60.1 vs. 72.17; P < 0.0001), and faster TUG times (P = 0.0104). ROM improvements were significant in both groups, with no statistically significant intergroup difference.
CONCLUSION: In this retrospective comparative study, the SV approach with surgeon-administered ACB was associated with better immediate post-operative analgesia and functional outcomes than the MP approach. The study cannot determine whether these differences were attributable to the surgical approach, ACB delivery, or both. Larger prospective, randomized studies with longer follow-up are warranted.

title: Study of Transdermal Buprenorphine Patch versus Oral Etoricoxib for Postoperative Pain Management after Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Randomized Comparative Open-label Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is a widely performed procedure for end-stage knee osteoarthritis, providing significant pain relief, improved joint function, and better quality of life. However, it is associated with substantial postoperative pain, which may delay mobilization, impair rehabilitation, prolong hospital stay, and increase the risk of chronic postoperative pain, thus making effective perioperative analgesia crucial for achieving optimal postoperative outcomes. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of transdermal buprenorphine patch versus oral etoricoxib for postoperative pain management in patients undergoing TKA, using Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) scores at rest and during movement for up to 1 week.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This randomized comparative study enrolled 88 patients of American Society of Anesthesiologists grade I/II after ethical approval. The patients were randomly allocated into two groups of 44 patients each. In Group A, patients received oral etoricoxib (90 mg), 1 h before surgery with a sip of water, and in Group B, patients received a transdermal buprenorphine patch (10 µg/h), 12 h before surgery. For statistical analysis, the Chi-square test and Student's t-test were used.
RESULTS: Statistically significant differences were observed in VAS scores (at rest and during movement), with Group B demonstrating significantly lower pain. Furthermore, rescue analgesic requirements and length of hospital stay were reduced significantly in Group B, thus indicating overall superior postoperative pain control.
CONCLUSION: Transdermal buprenorphine patch offers sustained analgesia (reduced VAS scores) with the potential for fewer systemic side effects, reduced need for additional opioid and rescue analgesic requirements, leading to shorter length of hospital stay.

title: Altered Cognitive Control and Cortical Oscillatory Dynamics in Athletes With ACL Reconstruction During Decision-Making Under Uncertainty.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury induces neuroplastic changes within the central nervous system (CNS) that may persist beyond reconstruction and rehabilitation.
PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose was to compare neurocognitive performance and cortical oscillatory activity between open-skill athletes (eg, soccer, basketball, or handball players) without ACL injury history and athletes with ACL reconstruction (ACLR) during a probabilistic go/no-go task. It was hypothesized that athletes with ACLR would exhibit poorer behavioral performance and less efficient oscillatory dynamics, particularly higher theta and lower suppression of beta and alpha power oscillations after goal stimulus onset.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: A total of 90 open-skill athletes (45 non-ACLR, 45 ACLR) performed a probabilistic go/no-go task while electroencephalographic recording was performed. Time-frequency analysis targeted midfrontal theta (4-7 Hz), left-lateralized central beta (15-25 Hz), and posterior alpha (8-12 Hz) oscillations during prestimulus and target stimulus windows. Linear mixed-effects models examined group differences in cognitive performance and oscillatory power.
RESULTS: Athletes with ACLR showed slower response times and lower accuracy (d = 0.75-1.09). Midfrontal theta power was attenuated for the ACLR group during the prestimulus phase (d = 0.60) yet elevated during target phase trials (d = 0.48), indicating a shift from proactive to reactive cognitive control in athletes with ACLR. Left-lateralized central beta (d = 0.61) and posterior alpha suppression (d = 0.55) were reduced, reflecting impaired motor cortical disinhibition and less efficient visual-attentional resource deployment, especially under high uncertainty conditions.
CONCLUSION: Athletes with ACLR showed persistent alterations in the cortical oscillatory mechanisms associated with conflict monitoring, motor preparation, and attentional allocation under uncertainty. These neurocognitive alterations may compromise adaptive motor responses in sport contexts characterized by high uncertainty and cognitive mental demand, potentially increasing reinjury risk. These findings support the integration of neurocognitive assessment into return-to-sport protocols.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Alterations in cortical oscillatory dynamics during decision-making under uncertainty may reflect reduced efficiency in cognitive control, motor preparation, and attentional allocation, which are not detected by standard assessments. Exercise professionals should consider integrating these assessments into return-to-sport protocols to address the persistent CNS alterations that may underlie reinjury risk in athletes with ACLR.

title: Low energy availability, disordered eating, exercise dependence, and injury prevalence in female CrossFit® athletes.
abstract: CrossFit® incorporates high-intensity, multimodal training with strong elements of community and competition. Despite known physical and psychological benefits, musculoskeletal injury prevalence ranges from 15 to 75%. Due to training demands, CrossFit® athletes may be at risk for low energy availability (LEA), disordered eating (DE), and exercise dependence (EXD), which may increase injury risk. Female CrossFit® participants (n = 198) completed an online survey including the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q), Exercise Dependence Scale (EDS-21), and Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q). Participants were classified as DE only, primary EXD, secondary EXD (DE + EXD), or control (no DE or EXD risk). Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. Overall, 37.8% of participants were at risk for LEA, 43.9% for DE, and 15.1% for EXD. Participants with secondary EXD had significantly (p < 0.001) higher EDE-Q global scores (3.9 ± 1.0) compared to primary EXD (1.4 ± 0.7) and control groups (1.0 ± 0.7). Additionally, 71.7% reported exercising despite injury, and 45.4% reported an injury within the past year. The prevalence of LEA, DE, and EXD was comparable to prior research; however, the high proportion of athletes continuing to train while injured suggests EXD-related behaviors may contribute to injury prevalence among CrossFit® athletes. These findings underscore the importance of early screening and education on adequate fueling and healthy training behaviors to support long-term health, performance, and injury prevention.

title: An Adaptive Knee Brace Is Associated With Improved Dynamic Stabilization Compared With a Standard Passive Brace in Anterior Cruciate Ligament-Deficient Men During a Functional Hop Task.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare the dynamic knee stabilization effects of an adaptive dynamic brace (ADB) with those of a standard passive brace in anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)-deficient men.
METHODS: ACL-deficient participants were included. The subjects performed 3 single-leg functional hop tests: drop jump, crossover hop, and 90° rotational hop. Each task was performed once while wearing the ADB and once while wearing a traditional passive brace. Three-dimensional kinematic data were collected using an 8-camera optoelectronic motion-capture system. Repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to evaluate the effects of brace condition and time. An a priori power analysis indicated that a minimum of 12 participants were required.
RESULTS: Twelve ACL-deficient participants were included (age: 30.2 ± 3.4 years; time since injury: 32 ± 6 months; ACL-Return to Sport after Injury score: 70 ± 3). No significant differences in knee flexion angles were observed between braces. Knee flexion during landing was significantly lower in the crossover hop compared with the drop jump and rotational hop tasks (P < .01). During the drop jump task, the ADB significantly reduced knee valgus angles (P < .01). In the crossover hop task, the ADB significantly reduced both knee valgus and rotational angles (P < .01). During the rotational hop task, a significant brace-by-time interaction was observed for knee valgus (P < .05) and rotational angles (P < .05).
CONCLUSIONS: The ADB showed improved dynamic stabilization particularly during high-risk landing and rotational movement compared with a standard passive brace.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The ADB may enhance the effectiveness of rehabilitation strategies in ACL-deficient individuals by improving dynamic knee stability during functional activities.

title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the effects of caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg on reactive blocking timing, block-jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses in elite female volleyball players under post-fatigue conditions.
METHODS: Fifteen elite female volleyball players completed a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study implemented with double-blinding procedures. Participants consumed placebo (PLA), caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 mg/kg (CAF3) or 6 mg/kg (CAF6), and were tested after supplementation and warm-up at PRE and immediately after a volleyball-specific repeated blocking fatigue protocol (POST). Primary outcomes were reactive blocking timing-chain indices and block-jump (BJ) peak power. Secondary outcomes included additional BJ mechanical variables and general jump measures from countermovement jump (CMJ) and drop jump (DJ) tests. Exploratory outcomes included synchronized surface electromyography (sEMG) variables of lower-limb muscles. Participant blinding was assessed after each visit.
RESULTS: Fatigue impaired jump-related performance across conditions (p < 0.05). For the primary outcomes, the descriptive decline in BJ peak power was 6.9% in CAF6 versus 13.9% in PLA; the adjusted POST comparison did not establish superiority of CAF6 over CAF3. For timing outcomes, overall sequence time increased by 18.4% in PLA, 6.4% in CAF3, and 3.0% in CAF6; CAF6 therefore showed the smallest descriptive deterioration in the integrated sequence measure, whereas CAF3 showed little change in the mean stationary and movement component times. CAF6 showed a reduction in mean stationary response time and the smallest increase in overall sequence time. For secondary outcomes, caffeine showed more favorable post-fatigue responses in selected CMJ/DJ measures, including CMJ mean propulsive power and DJ contact time (p < 0.05), and CAF6 showed greater preservation of selected stretch-shortening cycle-related mechanical measures, including DJ jump height and DJ vertical stiffness, than PLA (p < 0.05). In contrast, CMJ mRSI showed a divergent pattern and was not interpreted as evidence of caffeine-related attenuation of fatigue-induced decrements. Exploratory sEMG results showed smaller post-fatigue changes in selected frequency-domain and activation-timing variables under CAF6, particularly in measures related to extensor-muscle function. Participant masking was incomplete: perceived caffeine ingestion was reported in 0.0%, 53.3%, and 80.0% of PLA, CAF3, and CAF6 visits, respectively, and adverse effects were more frequent in CAF6.
CONCLUSIONS: The observed responses were outcome-specific: CAF6 showed a smaller decline in BJ peak power and the smallest increase in overall sequence time, whereas CAF3 showed little change in mean stationary and movement response times. These findings do not establish a generally preferable dose or a timing-stability advantage for CAF3. Incomplete participant masking limits attribution of the differences exclusively to caffeine dose.

title: Effects of Morning Strength and Power Priming Exercises on Afternoon Physical and Cognitive Performance in Male Rugby Union Players.
abstract: The objective of this study was to assess the effect of morning strength and power priming exercises on afternoon physical and cognitive performance in male rugby union players. On two occasions in a randomised, counterbalanced design, 25 male rugby union players completed morning physical (countermovement jump, 40 m linear sprint) and cognitive (rapid visual information processing; spatial working memory; paired associates of learning) assessments. Control (passive rest) or intervention (barbell back squat, 3 × 3 repetitions at 85% of one repetition maximum and barbell squat jump, 5 × 3 repetitions at 40% one repetition maximum) trials were implemented 5.5 h before afternoon assessments. Differences between morning and afternoon assessments were found in sprinting performance following intervention for 30 m fly (-0.08 ± 0.13 s, p = 0.004, ES: 0.615) and 40 m (-0.12 ± 0.17 s, p = 0.001, ES: 0.711) relative to control (0.03 ± 0.07 s, p = 0.022, ES: -0.476; 0.01 ± 0.09 s, p = 0.740, ES: -0.065, 30 m fly and 40 m, respectively). Afternoon countermovement jump flight time improved following intervention compared with control (2% vs. 0%, p = 0.012, ES: -0.53). No changes were found for cognitive assessments (p > 0.05). Morning strength and power priming exercises combining heavy-load traditional and light-load ballistic exercises effectively enhanced vertical jump and sprint performance, but not cognitive performance, in the afternoon in male rugby union players.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Safety of Tendon-Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cell Therapy in Equine Tendon and Ligament Injuries.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Equine tendinopathies and desmopathies are common musculoskeletal disorders characterized by a limited regenerative capacity and a high risk of recurrence. Tendon-derived mesenchymal stem cells (TDSCs) represent a promising regenerative therapy due to their immunomodulatory and pro-regenerative properties.
OBJECTIVES: This preliminary prospective clinical study aimed to evaluate the safety and potential efficacy of allogeneic post-mortem TDSCs, for the treatment of superficial digital flexor tendon (SDFT) and suspensory ligament (SL) injuries in horses.
METHODS: Nine horses were monitored longitudinally for up to 18 months following intralesional TDSC injection. Clinical outcome was assessed using subjective lameness evaluation, objective locomotion analysis with inertial sensors and standardized ultrasonographic examinations.
RESULTS: The treatment was well tolerated, with no major adverse effects, supporting the low immunogenicity of allogeneic TDSCs. Overall clinical improvement was observed during the follow-up period and was consistent with improved locomotor symmetry measured objectively. Ultrasonographic findings suggested favorable tissue remodeling, including a reduction in hypoechoic lesions and progressive reorganization of the fibrillar architecture. However, treatment responses were heterogeneous, with SDFT lesions showing earlier clinical and ultrasonographic improvement than SL lesions. Nevertheless, this trend was not reflected in long-term outcomes, as only two horses, both presenting SL lesions, returned to their previous level of competition without reported recurrence.
CONCLUSION: Allogeneic TDSCs appear to be a safe and promising therapeutic approach for equine tendon and ligament injuries. Nevertheless, their ability to reduce long-term recurrence remains uncertain and should be investigated in larger controlled clinical trials.

title: Genetic susceptibility to anterior cruciate ligament rupture in females: a systematic review of female-stratified candidate-gene evidence and the absence of genome-wide studies.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To systematically synthesise and critically appraise genetic association studies reporting female-stratified evidence for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture.
DESIGN: Systematic review.
DATA SOURCES: Web of Science, Scopus, Ovid MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to 21 December 2025, which was the predefined search date for this review.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR SELECTING STUDIES: Human genetic association studies reporting female-stratified ACL rupture outcomes or extractable female-only data were included. Studies reporting combined-sex analyses without extractable female data were excluded. Due to predefined heterogeneity in phenotypes, populations and genetic models, findings were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: 19 studies met the inclusion criteria, predominantly small candidate-gene case-control designs. Importantly, these publications did not represent 19 independent cohorts. The largest prospective cohort included 790 women at risk at baseline, of whom 58 sustained an incident ACL injury and 732 remained without incident injury. COL5A1 rs12722 was the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant. Positive single-variant estimates principally concerned CC homozygotes under a recessive model and arose from South African samples with documented participant reuse. Separate allelic associations were also reported. Independence of this signal was limited by probable cohort overlap, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence. Evidence for other collagen, proteoglycan, inflammatory and extracellular matrix remodelling genes was inconsistent. No female-stratified genome-wide association studies were identified.
CONCLUSIONS: COL5A1 rs12722 is the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant, but independent replication is not established. Positive recessive estimates concern CC homozygotes and should not be extended to heterozygotes. Small samples, participant reuse, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence limit certainty. Female-stratified associations do not establish sex-specific effects. Evidence derives predominantly from women of European ancestry, and generalisability to other ancestries remains unknown. Current findings do not support genetic screening for ACL rupture risk in female athletes; adequately powered, female-stratified genomic studies with rigorous phenotyping and independent replication across diverse ancestries are needed.

title: Changes in Hormone Cycles and Exercise Capacity During Testosterone Therapy in a Transmasculine Triathlete: A Case Study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The impact of testosterone therapy on the hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiology of transmasculine individuals is not well understood. Existing studies report limited metrics at large time intervals between data collection points.
METHODS: High-resolution temporal data were collected from a single amateur trans male triathlete over 13 months-including one baseline month and 12 months on testosterone therapy-to characterize hormone, strength, body composition, aerobic, and training load profiles.
RESULTS: Daily urine hormone monitoring revealed that progesterone and luteinizing hormone are the clearest metrics associated with cessation of menses. After 1 yr, the participant increased lean body mass by 12%, average hand grip strength by 16%, jump height by 16%, and average knee isometric strength by 18%, but did not lose fat mass or show changes in isokinetic knee strength. Fluctuations in running fitness and maximum oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 m a x ) were associated with both training and testosterone levels, with future work needed to untangle their relative contributions.
CONCLUSION: This study provides the most comprehensive characterization of the impacts of testosterone therapy on hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiological changes in a single person to date, as well as observations to help inform the design of larger cohort studies.

title: Indications, Techniques, and Outcomes of Meniscus Centralization for Root Tears and Meniscus Transplantation: An International Expert Consensus Statement.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To develop an expert consensus statement on the biomechanics, diagnosis, surgical indications and techniques, rehabilitation protocols, and postoperative outcomes of centralization procedures in meniscus root pathology and meniscal allograft transplantation.
METHODS: A working group generated 39 statements on meniscal centralization from previously published data for evaluation in a 3-round modified Delphi process. A panel of 22 international experts rated each statement on a 5-point Likert scale, and statements were retained, revised, or excluded according to predefined thresholds (≥75% agreement and <20% disagreement). Rounds 1 and 2 included both literature-derived items and open-ended responses, allowing panel members to propose additional statements.
RESULTS: Ultimately, 35 statements were retained, with 100% participation across all rounds. The expert panel reached consensus that centralization may be considered in the setting of root repair and meniscal allograft transplantation to reduce meniscal extrusion (ME), improve joint contact mechanics, potentially enhance root healing, and limit displacement of the repair. The expert panel suggested that the degree of ME may help guide decision-making and that successful outcomes after medial meniscus posterior root repair with centralization may be evaluated by changes in ME and degenerative progression. Medial meniscus posterior root centralization should be considered when ME on magnetic resonance imaging exceeds 3 mm, and lateral centralization should be considered for lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and >3 mm extrusion. Centralization was not recommended in advanced osteoarthritis. Panelists supported its use in symptomatic medial ME with varus deformity in combination with high tibial osteotomy. Transtibial tunnels, suture anchors, and hybrid constructs were all considered acceptable, provided that fixation is individualized to the location of ME and native meniscotibial anatomy and overtightening is avoided. The panel emphasized the need for long-term studies to confirm the durability and joint-protective benefits of centralization.
CONCLUSIONS: The panel supported consideration of meniscal centralization when magnetic resonance imaging shows extrusion greater than 3 mm in medial meniscus posterior root tears and in selected lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and extrusion greater than 3 mm. Its use was discouraged in the setting of advanced osteoarthritis, whereas a combined approach with high tibial osteotomy was supported in patients with symptomatic varus-associated medial ME. No single fixation construct was preferred; transtibial, anchor-based, and hybrid techniques were all considered acceptable. Emphasis was placed on individualized surgical decision-making and on avoiding overconstraint.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level V, expert opinion.

title: Pain Management in Elective Orthopaedic Surgery: A Delphi Consensus of the Academic Orthopaedic Consortium.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Pain management is a critical component of orthopaedic care, aimed at minimizing discomfort, facilitating recovery, and enhancing functional outcomes. The purpose of this study was to establish consensus statements through the Delphi process on pain management from preoperatively to postoperatively at the time of elective orthopaedic sports medicine and arthroplasty surgery.
METHODS: A consensus process using the Delphi technique was conducted. Thirty-seven orthopaedic surgeons, anaesthesiologist pain management physicians, and musculoskeletal researchers participated in these consensus statements. Consensus was defined as achieving 80 to 89% agreement, strong consensus was defined as 90 to 99% agreement, and unanimous consensus was indicated by 100% agreement with a proposed statement.
RESULTS: Of the 40 total questions and consensus statements in this group, four achieved unanimous consensus, 21 achieved strong consensus, 14 achieved consensus, and one did not reach any consensus.
CONCLUSION: The majority of statements reached some degree of consensus, with most achieving at least strong consensus. The statements that achieved unanimous consensus were on preoperative patient counselling for those with opioid addiction risk factors, including preoperative plans, preoperative education, frank discussions on expectations of pain after surgery, and pain management contracts. In addition, unanimous consensus was achieved that practices should have a standard opioid prescribing protocol to minimize prescribing, based on the procedure performed and with a maximum prescribing amount, and regarding the advantages of e-prescribing for opioids. Finally, unanimous consensus was determined that acetaminophen is always indicated, except when there is a medical contraindication such as liver impairment.

title: Dyslipidemia management in athletes: A comparative commentary on the 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline and contemporary sports cardiology recommendations.
abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of exercise-related sudden cardiac death in athletes older than 35 years, and dyslipidemia is one of its principal modifiable drivers. The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol introduces several advances directly relevant to athletes, including restored LDL-C treatment targets, universal lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] measurement, the PREVENT-ASCVD risk equations, expanded options for selective coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring, and a more aggressive approach to lipid-lowering therapy (LLT). However, sports cardiology guidelines and consensus statements offer important caveats that must be reconciled with these general-population recommendations: existing risk calculators, including PREVENT, do not reliably estimate cardiovascular risk in athletes, and routine CAC scoring is not recommended in athletes at low calculated risk. This commentary compares and contrasts general-population dyslipidemia recommendations with athlete-specific guidance from contemporary sports cardiology consensus documents, highlights recent evidence on Lp(a), wearable-derived training load, and risk score performance across the physical activity spectrum, and proposes a five-step clinical framework, refined to reflect athlete-specific risk stratification, for dyslipidemia evaluation and management in this population.

title: Clinical validation of a vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge plasma activation device for plasma-activated platelet-rich plasma preparation in osteoarthritis pain management.
abstract: Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has significant potential in biomedical applications. However, conventional plasma activation requires electrodes to contact a liquid directly, exposing it to the external environment. This conflicts with sterile, closed preparations required clinically. A vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma activation device addresses this need by using standard clinical blood collection tube walls as a dielectric barrier. Electrodes contact only the tube exterior, never the liquid inside, and activation requires simply inserting the tube into the reactor chamber. Applied to platelet-rich plasma (PRP) therapy for osteoarthritis (OA), the device produced plasma-activated PRP (PA-PRP) with enhanced platelet activation, increased levels of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β; 24%), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF; 37%), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; 32%), and broadly upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines. In the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse OA model, PA-PRP treatment was associated with improved gait parameters and lower cartilage degeneration scores relative to PRP treatment. Human OA cartilage explants showed greater matrix staining after PA-PRP treatment. In an exploratory, randomized, single-blind split-body study involving three patients, PA-PRP-treated knees, compared with contralateral PRP-treated knees, showed numerically larger improvements in visual analog scale (VAS) pain score, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score, and effusion volume at week 15, with no adverse events during observation. These clinical observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, as the sample size precludes reliable efficacy or comparative safety inferences. Together, findings support device feasibility and PA-PRP use in OA and provide a rationale for adequately powered studies.

title: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and its Implications for the Foot and Ankle Surgeon.
abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a syndrome caused by low energy availability that affects multiple physiologic systems in both male and female athletes. Stress fractures of the foot and ankle are often the first signs of RED-S; therefore, it is crucial that orthopedic surgeons are aware of and able to identify this disorder. This article focuses on RED-S and provides a framework for understanding the disorder, it's relevancy to the orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon, and offers suggestions for diagnostic strategies and treatment approaches that are imperative for safe return to play.

title: Adolescent Sports-Related Lower Extremity Pain and Overuse Injuries.
abstract: Adolescent participation in organized sports has increased substantially in recent decades, accompanied by a rising incidence of lower extremity pain and overuse injuries. Unique physiologic characteristics of the growing athlete, including open physes and periods of rapid skeletal maturation, combined with early sport specialization and increasing training demands, place adolescents at elevated risk for overuse conditions. This review examines common causes of sports-related lower extremity pain in adolescent athletes, including patellofemoral pain syndrome, Osgood-Schlatter disease, patellar tendinopathy, Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease, bone stress injuries, and symptomatic flexible flatfoot. For each condition, we review epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic considerations, and contemporary management strategies. Most overuse injuries in this population are diagnosed clinically and respond well to conservative treatment that emphasizes activity modification, progressive rehabilitation, and load management. Imaging should be used judiciously, primarily to confirm diagnosis or exclude alternative pathology. Emerging therapies, including biologic injections and bone stimulation modalities, show promise in select conditions but require further high-quality evidence before routine adoption. Prevention remains central to reducing injury burden. Gradual progression of training load, neuromuscular conditioning, nutritional optimization, and monitoring during growth spurts are key strategies. Increasing evidence also suggests that psychosocial factors may influence injury risk. A multidisciplinary approach involving clinicians, coaches, and strength and conditioning professionals is essential to promote safe, sustainable sports participation and long-term musculoskeletal health in adolescent athletes.
